question: Why should the final test set not guide repeated model or hyperparameter choices?
what_is_assessed: Understanding of overfitting to evaluation data and the distinct roles of validation and final testing.
short_answer: Repeatedly choosing models based on a test set makes the test set part of the learning process. The selected model can become tuned to quirks in that set, so its reported score is no longer an untouched estimate of performance on new data. I would use training data to fit, validation or cross-validation to compare choices, and reserve a representative test set for a final check. I would also keep preprocessing inside each training fold to avoid leakage.
deep_explanation: A test set is useful only to the extent that it is not repeatedly used to make modeling decisions. If many alternatives are tried and the best-looking test result is chosen, selection has implicitly used information from the test outcomes. A separate validation process supports model and parameter selection; a final held-out test set is evaluated after those choices are fixed. The split must reflect the data-generating structure: grouped users or time-ordered events may need group-aware or temporal splits rather than random shuffling. Preprocessing learned from data should be fit within each training fold, because fitting it before splitting can leak information. The scikit-learn guide explicitly warns against learning and testing on the same data and describes holding out test data.

Separates training, validation/model selection, and final evaluation.
Connects split design and preprocessing to leakage risk.
weak_answer_signals: Treats a single test score as an unbiased guarantee of deployment performance.
Uses the test set to repeatedly tune until the score improves.
common_mistakes: Calling the validation set an untouched final test after using it for selection.
Applying preprocessing to the full dataset before cross-validation.

question: A classifier has a lower Brier loss than a baseline. Does that prove its probabilities are better calibrated?

short_answer: No. Brier loss reflects calibration, discrimination, and outcome uncertainty together, so a lower value can result from stronger discrimination even if calibration worsens. Calibration should therefore be evaluated with a plot or decomposition suited to the question, not inferred from one aggregate score. Binning choices and sample counts also affect how stable a calibration curve appears.

short_answer: Use an inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted Brier score, with weights based on the estimated probability of remaining uncensored through the evaluation time. Do not label outcomes censored before one year as event-free or simply discard them without considering the resulting selection. The censoring distribution must be adequately specified, and extreme weights or poor support can make the estimate unstable.
deep_explanation: For a fixed horizon, a subject censored before that time has an unknown event status. IPCW uses the censoring distribution to reweight observations whose status is observed, approximating the target prediction error under the relevant censoring assumptions. The cited methodological study notes that consistency depends on correctly specifying the censoring distribution, so the metric is not assumption-free; check model fit, support, and weight stability.
strong_answer_signals: Uses an IPCW survival prediction metric for the fixed horizon.
Does not invent event status or ignore censoring without considering selection.
States that the censoring distribution must be estimated adequately and checks weight stability.
weak_answer_signals: Counts everyone censored before the horizon as event-free.
Drops censored observations and assumes the remaining sample is representative.
common_mistakes: Treating IPCW as assumption-free.
Ignoring very large weights or weak support in the estimated censoring distribution.

follow_ups.question: What probability appears in the censoring weight?
follow_ups.short_answer: The estimated probability of remaining uncensored through the evaluation time.

follow_ups.question: What model issue can destabilize IPCW?
follow_ups.short_answer: A misspecified censoring distribution, weak support, or extreme weights.

question: A study is not statistically significant, so an analyst reports 18% observed power and concludes that no effect exists. How would you respond?
what_is_assessed: Whether the candidate understands the limits of post-hoc power and communicates uncertainty without treating a nonsignificant result as evidence of no effect.
short_answer: That conclusion is not justified. Post-hoc power calculated from the observed result is largely a transformation of the p-value and adds no independent evidence that the effect is absent. Report the effect estimate and confidence interval, compare the plausible effects with a pre-defined threshold for practical importance, and use a prospective power analysis when planning a future study.
deep_explanation: The cited methodological review explains that post-hoc power is a monotone function of the observed p-value and provides no additional helpful information. A nonsignificant result does not establish that the effect is zero. The estimate and its uncertainty interval show which effect sizes remain compatible with the data; if the goal is to establish practical equivalence, define an acceptable margin and use an appropriate equivalence procedure. Power calculations are most useful prospectively, under explicit assumptions about the effect and design.
strong_answer_signals: Rejects the claim that low observed power proves absence of an effect.
Explains that post-hoc power adds no independent information beyond the observed test result.
Uses an effect estimate and uncertainty interval to discuss practical implications.
weak_answer_signals: Treats low observed power as proof of a null effect.
Claims a nonsignificant p-value demonstrates no meaningful difference.
common_mistakes: Using post-hoc power to explain away an inconclusive result.
Failing to define what effect size would be practically negligible.

follow_ups.question: What should be reported instead of observed power?
follow_ups.short_answer: The effect estimate and its confidence interval, interpreted against a meaningful effect threshold.

follow_ups.question: When is a power calculation most useful?
follow_ups.short_answer: Prospectively, when planning a study under explicit design and effect-size assumptions.

question: A Bayesian model has converged chains and acceptable R-hat values. What check would help determine whether it reproduces important features of the observed data?
what_is_assessed: Whether the candidate distinguishes computational convergence from model adequacy and uses replicated data to evaluate fit.
short_answer: Run posterior predictive checks: simulate replicated datasets from the fitted model's posterior predictive distribution, then compare relevant summaries or visual patterns with the observed data. Good convergence shows that sampling behaved acceptably; it does not show that the model captures the data-generating patterns that matter.
deep_explanation: The Stan User's Guide describes posterior predictive checking as simulating new replicated datasets from fitted model parameters and comparing statistics of those replications with the same statistics from observed data. Choose checks tied to the application, such as means, dispersion, tails, zero counts, or group-level patterns. A mismatch can reveal model inadequacy even when the sampler converges; a match on selected summaries is useful evidence but does not prove the model is correct in every respect.
strong_answer_signals: Separates sampler convergence from whether the model reproduces the data.
Simulates replicated data under the fitted posterior.
Chooses checks that reflect meaningful features of the application.
weak_answer_signals: Treats good R-hat values as proof that the model fits.
Checks only a generic average without considering the data's important structure.
common_mistakes: Using posterior predictive checks as a guarantee of model truth.
Choosing diagnostics after seeing results without explaining which failures matter.

follow_ups.question: What is compared in a posterior predictive check?
follow_ups.short_answer: Statistics or patterns from replicated datasets and the corresponding observed data.

follow_ups.question: Do good convergence diagnostics establish model adequacy?
follow_ups.short_answer: No. They assess computation, not whether the model captures relevant data patterns.

question: An experiment's primary metric is total clicks divided by total impressions. The analyst computes separate confidence intervals for clicks and impressions, then divides their endpoints. What should change?
what_is_assessed: Whether the candidate treats a ratio metric as a joint estimand and accounts for dependence between its numerator and denominator.
short_answer: Do not divide the endpoints of two separate intervals. Define the ratio estimand and estimate its uncertainty with a ratio-aware method, such as a delta-method calculation or a user-level bootstrap that resamples the numerator and denominator together at the randomization unit. Their covariance can affect the variance of the ratio.
deep_explanation: Online-experiment ratio metrics are often ratios of sums of additive metrics, such as clicks over impressions. The cited analysis models numerator and denominator behavior jointly, includes their covariance, and derives inference using the delta method. A valid analysis should preserve the pairing and randomization structure, state whether the estimand is a ratio of totals or an average of per-user ratios, and avoid treating the two components as independent unless that assumption is justified.
strong_answer_signals: Rejects dividing endpoints from separate confidence intervals.
Recognizes covariance between numerator and denominator.
Names a joint method such as the delta method or a design-respecting user-level bootstrap.
States the ratio estimand and randomization unit.
weak_answer_signals: Treats numerator and denominator uncertainty as independent by default.
Changes between a ratio of totals and an average of user-level ratios without stating it.
common_mistakes: Resampling clicks and impressions independently and losing their pairing.
Reporting a ratio without defining its aggregation or denominator.

follow_ups.question: Why can numerator-denominator covariance matter?
follow_ups.short_answer: It contributes to the sampling variance of their ratio.

follow_ups.question: What must a bootstrap preserve?
follow_ups.short_answer: The paired numerator and denominator observations and the experiment's randomization unit.

question: A small binomial sample has a proportion near zero, and the normal-approximation confidence interval extends below zero. What should you do?
what_is_assessed: Whether the candidate recognizes boundary and coverage problems with the Wald interval and selects a method appropriate for binomial data.
short_answer: Do not simply clip the interval at zero. The Wald approximation can perform poorly for small samples or proportions near the boundaries. Use a binomial interval such as the Wilson score, Agresti-Coull, or an exact method, and report the successes and denominator. Choose based on the design and desired coverage properties rather than treating one interval as universally best.
deep_explanation: The NIST technical note reviews confidence intervals for binomial proportions, including Wald, Wilson, Agresti-Coull, and exact methods. It explains that normal-approximation intervals rely on large-sample behavior and that Wilson or Agresti-Coull may be preferable to the standard Wald interval in some smaller-sample settings. The interval should reflect the binomial model and sampling design; clipping an invalid Wald endpoint does not repair its coverage properties.
strong_answer_signals: Identifies the normal/Wald approximation as problematic near boundaries or with limited data.
Names a score or exact interval as an alternative.
Reports the numerator and denominator and avoids a universal cutoff claim.
weak_answer_signals: Clips the endpoint and assumes the resulting interval is valid.
Uses a normal interval without checking sample size or the boundary case.
common_mistakes: Treating Wilson as universally optimal for every design.
Reporting a percentage without its denominator.

follow_ups.question: Why is clipping the Wald interval not enough?
follow_ups.short_answer: It does not correct the method's coverage behavior.

follow_ups.question: What should accompany a small-sample proportion?
follow_ups.short_answer: The number of successes, total trials, and a binomial-appropriate uncertainty interval.

topic: Ecological inference and levels of analysis
question: A county-level analysis finds that areas with higher average education have lower disease rates. Can you conclude that individuals with more education had lower disease risk?
what_is_assessed: Whether the candidate distinguishes a population-level association from an individual-level relationship and avoids an unsupported cross-level inference.
short_answer: No—not from the county-level association alone. Many different individual-level relationships can produce the same aggregate pattern. State whether the target is a population or contextual effect; if you need an individual-level conclusion, use individual-level data or an ecological-inference method with explicit assumptions.
deep_explanation: The cited review defines ecological inference as drawing conclusions about individual-level behavior from aggregate data and explains that many individual relationships can be consistent with the same aggregate observations. It also cautions against labeling every ecological study a fallacy: a population-level or contextual question can be valid when the analysis does not claim an individual-level result. The key is to match the unit of analysis to the conclusion and make any cross-level assumptions explicit.
strong_answer_signals: Rejects the individual-level conclusion from aggregate data alone.
Explains that multiple individual patterns may produce the same group-level association.
Distinguishes a population-level target from an individual-level inference.
weak_answer_signals: Assumes a group-level relationship necessarily holds for individuals.
Dismisses all ecological analyses as invalid regardless of their target.
common_mistakes: Confusing an ecological association with an individual causal effect.
Ignoring the unit at which exposure and outcome were measured.

follow_ups.question: When is an ecological study not making this error?
follow_ups.short_answer: When its target is a population or contextual effect and it does not infer an individual-level relationship.

follow_ups.question: What can support an individual-level conclusion?
follow_ups.short_answer: Individual-level data or an ecological-inference model with justified assumptions.
